<div class="exercise" id="exercise-1">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}\setcounter{exercise}{0}
\begin{exercise}
\label{exer:reverse-from-split}Show that $\reverseterm$ can be implemented by a polyregular term that does not use it.
\end{exercise}
{{< /latex >}}
<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}
\noindent\textbf{Solution.}\quad We first implement a version of the head function, which returns the singleton list containing the first element of a list if it is non-empty, and the empty list otherwise.
\begin{align*}
A^* \xrightarrow {\unconsterm} \onetype + A \times A^* \xrightarrow {\either {\emptyterm} {\fstterm;\pureterm}} A^*
\end{align*}
Using the above function, we define reverse to be the following composition
\begin{safeTikzcdDisplay}
A^* 
\ar[d,"{\splitterm}"]
\& 
{[1,2,3]}
\ar[d,mapsto] \\
(A^* \times A^*)^* 
\ar[d, "{\sndterm^*}"]
\&
{[([1,2,3],[]),  ([1,2],[3]),  ([1],[2,3]),  ([],[1,2,3])]}
\ar[d,mapsto] \\
A^{**}
\ar[d, "{\text{(the head function above)}^*}"]
\&
{[[], [3], [2,3], [1,2,3]]}
\ar[d,mapsto] \\
A^{**}
\ar[d, "{\concatterm}"]
\&
{[[], [3], [2], [1]]}
\ar[d,mapsto] \\
A^*
\&
{[3,2,1]}.
\end{safeTikzcdDisplay}
{{< /latex >}}
</div>
</details>
</div>
<div class="exercise" id="exercise-2">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}\setcounter{exercise}{1}
\begin{exercise}
\label{exer:split-triple}
Write a polyregular term which defines the following variant of the split function 
\begin{align*}
A^* & \to (A^* \times A \times A^*)^*\\
[a_1,\ldots,a_n] & \mapsto [t_1,\ldots,t_n] \quad \text{where } t_i = ([a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1}],a_i,[a_{i+1},\ldots,a_n]).
\end{align*}
\end{exercise}
{{< /latex >}}
<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}
\noindent\textbf{Solution.}\quad %     A type $\onetype + A$ can be seen as a variant of the Maybe monad, where we have a possibly undefined value of type $A$. Another way to implement this construction is by using $A^*$, with the empty list representing the undefined value, a list of length one representing a defined value, and lists of greater length never used. This representation is implemented by the function 
% \begin{align*}
% \onetype + A  \xrightarrow{\mathtt{maybe}} A^*,
% \end{align*}
% which can be easily implemented by a regular term.
% Using  distributitivy, the list deconstructor, and the above representation of the Maybe monad, we can implement the following function
% \begin{align*}
% A^* \times A^* & \to  (A^* \times A \times A^*)^* \\
% (w,[a_1,\ldots,a_n]) & \mapsto 
% \begin{cases}
%     [(w,a_1,[a_2,\ldots,a_n])] & \text{if $n \ge 1$} \\
%     [] & \text{otherwise}.
% \end{cases}
% \end{align*}
% The function in the statement of the exercise is obtained by applying first split, then the above function to each list element, followed by $\concatterm$. 
This is the following composition. The final reversal is needed because $\splitterm$ lists the splits with the prefix getting shorter, so that without it the triples would be produced in the order $t_n,\ldots,t_1$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A^*
\ar[d, "\splitterm"]
\\
(A^* \times A^*)^* 
\ar[d, "{(\idterm \times \unconsterm)^*}"]
\\
(A^* \times (\onetype + A \times A^*))^* 
\ar[d, "{(\distrterm)^*}"]
\\
(A^* \times \onetype + A^* \times A \times A^*)^* 
\ar[d,"{\text{function from \cref{exer:filter-plus}}}"]
\\
(A^* \times A \times A^*)^* 
\ar[d,"{\reverseterm}"]
\\
(A^* \times A \times A^*)^* 
\end{tikzcd}
\]
{{< /latex >}}
</div>
</details>
</div>
<div class="exercise" id="exercise-3">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}\setcounter{exercise}{2}
\begin{exercise}
\label{exer:block-from-split}Show that $\blockterm$ can be implemented by a polyregular term that does not use it (or reverse).
\end{exercise}
{{< /latex >}}
<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
% context stamp f3066681
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{3}\setcounter{theorem}{16}
\noindent\textbf{Solution.}\quad Since pairing is available, we can separately define the two components of the output of $\blockterm$. The first component is a list of type $A^*$ which contains the prefix up to (but not including) the first $B$, and the second component is a list of type $(B \times A^*)^*$ that describes the blocks which begin with occurrences of $B$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item To define the first component of the output, we  begin with an auxiliary  function of type $(A+B)^* \to \onetype + \onetype$ which tells us if the input list uses only elements of type $A$. This function is implemented (without using $\blockterm$) by keeping only the elements of type $B$ and then checking emptiness. Once this auxiliary function is defined, we use the following composition to define the first component of the output of $\blockterm$. As in \cref{exer:split-triple}, a reversal is needed at the end, because $\splitterm$ enumerates the all-$A$ prefixes from the longest to the shortest; this does not conflict with the restriction in the statement, since \cref{exer:reverse-from-split} implements reversal without using it.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
(A + B)^* 
\ar[d, "\splitterm"] 
\\
((A+B)^* \times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d, "{(\text{(auxiliary function)} \times \idterm)^*}"]
\\
((\onetype + \onetype) \times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d,"{\distlterm^*}"]
\\
( (A+B)^* + (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d,"{\text{function from \cref{exer:filter-plus}}}"]
\\
(A+B)^{**}
\ar[d, "{\unconsterm^*}"]
\\ 
(\onetype + (A+B) \times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d, "{\text{function from \cref{exer:filter-plus}}}"]
\\
((A+B)\times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d, "{\fstterm^*}"]
\\
(A+B)^*
\ar[d, "{\text{function from \cref{exer:filter-plus}}}"]
\\
A^*
\ar[d, "{\reverseterm}"]
\\
A^*
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item The second component of the output is defined using the following composition:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
(A+B)^*
\ar[d, "{\text{function from \cref{exer:split-triple}}}"]
\\
((A+B)^* \times (A+B) \times (A+B)^*)^* 
\ar[d, "\sndterm^*"]
\\
( (A+B) \times (A+B)^*)^* 
\ar[d,"\distlterm^*"]
\\
(A \times (A+B)^* + B \times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d, "{\text{function from \cref{exer:filter-plus}}}"]
\\
(B \times (A+B)^*)^*
\ar[d, "{(\idterm \times \text{first component})^*}"]
\\
(B \times A^*)^*
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\end{enumerate}
{{< /latex >}}
</div>
